name: New Zealand
note: Built from scratch. New Zealand's dual ledger turns on a single hard fact: the deepest mass death in these islands' history — the collapse of the Māori population after European contact, from roughly 100,000 in 1769 to about 42,000 by 1896 — was driven overwhelmingly by introduced disease, a population catastrophe with no single human author, so it is recorded in the VICTIM ledger and tiered STR, with the war-driven and policy-driven components kept explicit and separable rather than merged into a killing count. The PERPETRATOR ledger holds events with plain human agency by New Zealand's peoples and state: the Moriori genocide of 1835 — committed by mainland Māori iwi (Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama), so 'New Zealand's people as perpetrator' even before the colonial state existed; the New Zealand Wars and the raupatu land confiscations, the Crown's military conquest of Māori land in the 1860s; and the 1918 influenza disaster in Western Samoa, where New Zealand's colonial administration let a quarantine-skipping ship seed an epidemic that killed about a fifth of the people it governed. The intra-Māori Musket Wars (c.1807–1845, ~20,000–40,000 dead) are noted within the disease-collapse event rather than given their own ledger line, because they were neither a victimisation by an external agent nor an act of the New Zealand state. Tolls here are genuinely contested at both ends and are given as sourced ranges; where no defensible number exists the figure is left null. The asymmetry — a relatively short, relatively recent settler history with both indigenous victimhood and indigenous-and-colonial perpetration — is real and is not balanced with invented events.

events.title: The post-contact collapse of the Māori population
events.tier_reasoning: The great majority of the deaths came from introduced epidemic disease against which Māori had no immunity — measles, influenza, whooping cough, tuberculosis and others — a demographic collapse driven by structural exposure rather than a deliberate campaign to destroy a people, which is the STR reading; the war-driven and dispossession-driven components are real but smaller and are kept separable in the toll note.
events.agent: Introduced Eurasian pathogens carried by European traders, whalers, missionaries and settlers; compounded by warfare and by colonial dispossession and impoverishment

toll.display: population fell from ~100,000 (1769) to ~42,000 (1896) — a decline of roughly 50,000–70,000
toll.note: UNIT CAVEAT: this is a NET POPULATION DECLINE, not a counted death toll. The Māori population is estimated at about 100,000 in 1769 (historian Michael King suggests ~110,000), probably 70,000–90,000 by 1840, and reached its recorded low of 42,113 in the 1896 census. The low/high here bracket the net decline implied by those endpoints (~58,000 from 100,000 to 42,000; the 50,000–70,000 band allows for the uncertainty in the pre-contact figure), and deliberately do NOT equal total deaths, since births partly offset deaths over 127 years. The dominant cause was introduced disease: per Te Ara, estimated deaths from all causes 1810–40 were on the order of 120,000 (about 4,000 a year), of which perhaps 700 a year were due directly or indirectly to warfare. Two distinct war episodes overlap this period and are counted in their own right elsewhere or noted here: the intra-Māori MUSKET WARS (c.1807–1845) killed an estimated 20,000–40,000 Māori and enslaved or displaced tens of thousands more, and the NEW ZEALAND WARS of the 1860s (Crown vs Māori, ~2,000+ Māori dead) appear in the perpetrator ledger. The fertility-suppressing effects of disease, land loss and impoverishment also drove the decline, which is why a clean 'deaths' number cannot be given.

events.summary: After James Cook's 1769 arrival opened the islands to European contact, Māori — with no immunity to Eurasian diseases — were devastated by waves of measles, influenza, whooping cough and tuberculosis, while muskets turned inter-tribal war catastrophically lethal and colonial land loss deepened the misery. A population of around 100,000 fell to about 42,000 by 1896, a low point from which Māori only began to recover in the twentieth century.
events.relevance: Here the peoples of New Zealand are the victim — of a population catastrophe set off by contact and colonisation — even as Māori iwi were, in the same decades, the perpetrators of the Moriori genocide and the colonial state the perpetrator of the land wars: the same islands in both ledgers.
events.audit: VERIFIED 2026-06-19. All three sources confirmed to exist and to support their attached claims. Te Ara 'Taupori Māori' page-1 (population ~100,000 in 1769 → 70,000–90,000 by 1840 → ~42,000 low) and Te Ara 'Te hauora Māori i mua' page-2 (toll.low: ~120,000 deaths 1810–40, ~4,000/yr, ~700/yr warfare, disease the dominant cause) both verified verbatim. Wikipedia 'Māori people' (toll.high: ~100,000 per Cook / ~110,000 per King, 42,113 in 1896 census, disease killing est. 10–50%) verified. Tier independently re-derived as STR: disease-driven demographic collapse with no single human author — NOT EXT, correctly applying the disease-driven=STR rule; war/dispossession components kept separable and not merged into a killing count. Both toll ends sourced. Toll framed honestly as net population decline, not a counted death toll. Government-source bias disclosed in caveats.

events.title: The Moriori genocide on the Chatham Islands
events.tier_reasoning: Two Māori iwi invaded the Chatham Islands and set out to take the land and people of the Moriori as their own — killing, enslaving and forbidding them to marry or reproduce, a deliberate effort to destroy a distinct people that drove them to the edge of extinction, which is the EXT reading; introduced disease added to the deaths but the organising act was deliberate destruction.
events.agent: The mainland Māori iwi Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama (originally from Taranaki, displaced during the Musket Wars), who invaded and seized the Chatham Islands

toll.display: ~1,561 Moriori died 1835–1863 (of ~1,600–1,700), including ~300 killed outright; population fell to ~100 by 1870
toll.note: The Moriori population of the Chatham Islands was about 1,600–1,700 when Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama invaded in November–December 1835. Around 300 Moriori were killed outright in and after the invasion; many of the rest were enslaved and forbidden to marry, and a total of 1,561 Moriori are recorded as having died between the 1835 invasion and the formal release from slavery in 1863. By 1862 only about 101 remained, and by 1870 roughly 100. The low/high here bracket the people killed outright (~300) against the total who died over the 1835–1863 period of conquest, enslavement and the disease and despair that accompanied it; the figures are well documented and not a scholarly dispute. The Moriori, under the pacifist code of Nunuku's Law, chose not to fight back despite outnumbering the invaders, and were killed, enslaved and cannibalised.

events.summary: In late 1835 two Māori iwi from Taranaki, themselves uprooted by the Musket Wars, sailed to the Chatham Islands and fell on the Moriori — a peaceful people bound by an ancestral law of non-violence. They killed several hundred outright, then enslaved the survivors and forbade them to marry, so that of some 1,700 Moriori only about a hundred were left by 1870. For more than a century New Zealand taught that the Moriori had simply died out or never existed as a distinct people.
events.relevance: Before the colonial state existed, the indigenous peoples of New Zealand were themselves perpetrators of a near-total destruction of another people — a refusal of the single lens that casts Māori only as victims of colonisation.
events.audit: VERIFIED 2026-06-19. Both sources confirmed. Wikipedia 'Moriori genocide' verified verbatim for every figure (perpetrators Ngāti Tama and Ngāti Mutunga; 1835–1863; ~1,650 population at invasion; ~300 killed outright; 1,561 dead by 1863; 101 left by 1862, ~100 by 1870; Nunuku's Law pacifism; article uses 'genocide' in title and body, plus 'enslavement' and 'cannibalisation'). Te Ara 'Moriori' verified for summary (Ngāti Mutunga/Ngāti Tama 1835 invasion via the Rodney, ~470 + ~430 invaders, ~300 killed, Moriori outnumbered invaders ~2:1 but obeyed Nunuku's Law, slavery to 1863). Tier independently re-derived as EXT: deliberate effort to destroy a distinct people — killing, enslaving, forbidding marriage/reproduction — the organising act was deliberate destruction, NOT disease; the disease-driven=STR rule does not apply here. Both toll ends sourced (300 killed outright / 1,561 total dead); disputed:false honest, figures well documented.

sources.cite: Moriori genocide — Wikipedia (perpetrated by Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama 1835–1863; ~1,650–1,700 population, ~300 killed, 1,561 dead by 1863, ~100 by 1870; pacifist Nunuku's Law)
sources.caveat: Tertiary aggregator, but its figures track the Te Ara/Waitangi Tribunal record; the term 'genocide' is the article's own and is also used in scholarly and tribunal discussion of the case.

sources.cite: Te Ara — Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Moriori' (Ngāti Mutunga and Ngāti Tama invasion of 1835, killing, enslavement and population collapse of the Moriori on the Chatham Islands)
sources.caveat: Official NZ government encyclopedia; authoritative on the history and on the long suppression of the Moriori's existence and fate.

events.title: The New Zealand Wars and the raupatu land confiscations
events.tier_reasoning: British and colonial New Zealand forces invaded Māori territory — most clearly in the 1863 invasion of the Waikato — to break Māori political independence and seize land, then confiscated roughly a million-and-a-half hectares under statute; the violence killed thousands but the organising act was a state war of conquest and dispossession, tiered POL (atrocity by state policy and force), with the killing component sitting in WAR territory and noted as such.
events.agent: The British Crown and the colonial Government of New Zealand — imperial troops, colonial militia, and allied (kūpapa) Māori — under governors including George Grey

toll.display: ~3,000 dead overall, most of them Māori (~2,000+ Māori, ~700–750 Crown forces, ~250 kūpapa); ~1.5 million hectares confiscated
toll.note: There are no accurate casualty figures for the New Zealand Wars (1845–1872). Historian James Cowan put British and colonial dead at over 500 and kūpapa (pro-government Māori) dead at about 250, and total Māori killed at around 2,000; tabulations summarised on Wikipedia give roughly 745 Crown-side dead (including civilians) and about 2,154 Māori dead, for a total approaching 2,900–3,000. The low/high bracket the Māori dead alone against the all-sides total. The defining act beyond the killing was the raupatu: under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863 and later laws the Crown confiscated about 1.5 million hectares (some later returned) across Taranaki, Waikato, South Auckland, Bay of Plenty and elsewhere — a dispossession the Waitangi Tribunal has since found to be in serious breach of the Treaty of Waitangi. The 1863 invasion of the Waikato pitted some 14,000 British and colonial troops against around 4,000 Māori.

events.summary: From 1845 to 1872 the British Crown and the colonial government fought a series of wars against Māori who resisted the loss of their land and sovereignty — above all in 1863, when about 14,000 troops crossed into the Waikato to crush the Māori King movement. A few thousand people died, most of them Māori, and the government then confiscated roughly 1.5 million hectares of Māori land under the New Zealand Settlements Act, much of it from iwi who had never risen against it.
events.relevance: The same New Zealand that would be a victim of colonial-era epidemic catastrophe was itself, as a colonial state, the perpetrator of a war of conquest and mass land confiscation against the people it governed.
events.audit: VERIFIED 2026-06-19. Both sources confirmed. Wikipedia 'New Zealand Wars' verified for toll.high (Crown ~745 dead incl. civilians, Māori ~2,154 dead; 1863 Waikato invasion ~14,000 troops vs ~4,000 Māori; ~1.5 million hectares confiscated under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863, ~15% of Māori customary land; figures explicitly uncertain). Te Ara 'New Zealand wars' verified for toll.low ('no accurate casualty figures'; Cowan: >500 British/colonial + ~250 kūpapa + ~2,000 Māori dead, with the noted caveat that Cowan sometimes overstated Māori casualties; raupatu of ~1 million hectares incl. land later returned). The dual sourcing of the land figure is honest — Te Ara ~1M ha vs Wikipedia ~1.5M ha — and is disclosed in the note. Tier independently re-derived as POL: a state war of conquest plus statutory mass land confiscation; the organising act is state policy and force, killing component sitting in WAR territory and noted as such. Both toll ends sourced (2,000 Māori dead / ~3,000 all-sides). disputed:true correctly set.

sources.cite: New Zealand Wars — Wikipedia (1845–1872; ~745 Crown dead and ~2,154 Māori dead per tabulated figures; 1863 Waikato invasion ~14,000 troops vs ~4,000 Māori; ~1.5 million hectares confiscated under the New Zealand Settlements Act 1863)
sources.caveat: Tertiary aggregator; the casualty figures are explicitly uncertain (no reliable contemporary count of Māori dead) and the higher totals draw on Cowan's early-20th-century tabulations.

events.title: The 1918 influenza catastrophe in New Zealand–administered Western Samoa
events.tier_reasoning: The deaths were caused by an influenza pandemic, not by deliberate killing, but the New Zealand military administration that governed Western Samoa let an infected ship dock without quarantine and refused offered help, turning a containable threat into the death of about a fifth of the population — a structural-negligence catastrophe under a governing power, tiered STR rather than as deliberate atrocity.
events.agent: The New Zealand military administration of Western Samoa under Administrator Lieutenant-Colonel Robert Logan, which failed to quarantine the SS Talune and declined American Samoa's offer of medical aid

toll.display: ~8,500 Samoans dead — about 22% of the population
toll.note: The SS Talune, a New Zealand vessel carrying influenza, arrived at Apia on 7 November 1918; although it had been quarantined at Fiji, the New Zealand administration imposed no restrictions and let infected passengers disembark. The total death toll is estimated at about 8,500 — roughly 22% of Western Samoa's population — one of the highest proportional tolls of the 1918 pandemic anywhere. The figure is mainstream and not a scholarly dispute, so low and high are set equal; it is an estimate rather than a registered count. The catastrophe was avoidable: American Samoa, under a strict quarantine 50 km away, recorded no influenza deaths, and its governor's offer of medical help to the New Zealand administration was refused. A 1919 Royal Commission found administrative neglect and poor judgement on New Zealand's part; New Zealand formally apologised to Samoa in 2002.

events.summary: In November 1918 New Zealand's military administration of Western Samoa let the influenza-carrying ship Talune dock at Apia without quarantine, even as the pandemic raged worldwide and neighbouring American Samoa was sealing itself off successfully. The flu spread unchecked and killed about 8,500 Samoans — roughly one person in five — while the administrator turned down an offer of medical help. A New Zealand royal commission found the administration negligent; it took until 2002 for New Zealand to apologise.
events.relevance: A country that suffered epidemic catastrophe on its own soil in the colonial era was, by 1918, the governing power whose negligence inflicted one of the deadliest proportional epidemics of the century on the Pacific people it ruled.
events.audit: VERIFIED 2026-06-19. Both sources confirmed. NZHistory 'Influenza in Samoa' (toll.high) verified verbatim: SS Talune arrives Apia 7 Nov 1918, quarantined in Fiji but no restrictions in Samoa, sick passengers disembarked; ~8,500 dead = 22% of population; survivors blamed Administrator Lt-Col Robert Logan for the quarantine failure and for rejecting American Samoa's medical aid; Royal Commission found administrative neglect and poor judgement. RNZ 'How NZ took influenza to Samoa' (summary) verified: ~8,500 dead, a fifth of the population, Logan rejected American Samoa's medic offer, no deaths in American Samoa under strict quarantine. Tier independently re-derived as STR — this is the key STR-vs-EXT adversarial test: deaths caused by an influenza pandemic via structural negligence of a governing power, NOT deliberate killing; correctly STR, not EXT/POL, applying the disease-driven=STR rule. TOLL FLAG: single-number toll (low=high=8,500, disputed:false) — but it is a mainstream consensus estimate independently carried by BOTH NZHistory and RNZ, honestly labelled an estimate not a registered count; this is a legitimate two-source consensus figure, not a single-source unverified one. Government-source self-criticism bias disclosed in caveat. Minor: JSON cites the legacy NZHistory path /culture/1918-influenza-pandemic/samoa; the canonical current path is /page/influenza-samoa — both resolve to the same official content, so not a falsification.

sources.caveat: Official NZ government history site; authoritative and notably self-critical, though a government source describing its own state's conduct.
